chunks: Yaqub ibn Yazid from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"The one who was in charge of the camels of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was Najjah ibn Junayb al-Khuza'i al-Aslami, and the one who shaved the head of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) on the Day of al-Hudaybiyyah was Kharash ibn Umayyah al-Khuza'i, and the one who shaved the head of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) during his Hajj was Ma'mar ibn 'Abdillah ibn Harithah ibn Nadr ibn 'Awf ibn 'Awij ibn 'Adi ibn Ka'b."

He said, "And when it was during the Hajj of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), while he was shaving him, the Quraysh said, 'O Ma'mar, the ear of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) is in your hand, and in your hand is the razor.' So Ma'mar said, 'By Allah, I consider it a great favor from Allah upon me.'

He said, "And Ma'mar ibn 'Abdillah was the one who saddled the camel for the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'O Ma'mar, indeed the saddle will loosen tonight.' Ma'mar said, 'My father and mother be sacrificed for you, I have tightened it as I always tighten it, but some of those who envied my position with you, O Messenger of Allah, wanted you to replace me.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said, 'I would not do that.'

key_terms.اَلْحُدَيْبِيَةِ: Al-Hudaybiyyah, a location near Mecca famous for the treaty of peace
key_terms.بُدْنِ: Camels used for sacrifice or transport

ai.seo_question: Who shaved the Prophet's head and handled his camel during Hajj?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the specific companions who served the Prophet in intimate capacities, such as shaving his head during the Farewell Pilgrimage and handling his camel, illustrating the honor (*fada'il*) they placed on these humble duties. It further contextualizes the loosening of the saddle not merely as a physical occurrence but as a subtle manifestation of the envy (*hasad*) of others, a theme the Prophet acknowledges with grace, reinforcing the Shia emphasis on the spiritual status of those close to him.
